analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to count patients' copay assistance toward deductibles and out-of-pocket limits.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to stop health plans from ignoring patients' copay assistance sat in the Senate health committee for over a year, got one hearing, and has not received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Many people with expensive prescriptions get help paying for them from charities or drug manufacturers, but many health plans refuse to count that help toward the patient's deductible or annual out-of-pocket maximum — a practice known as a "copay accumulator." This bill would require plans to count that assistance, so patients could reach their out-of-pocket cap and stop paying for covered drugs. It would take effect for plan years starting in 2026 or later.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with high-cost prescriptions — especially specialty drugs for cancer, multiple sclerosis, and rare diseases — who receive copay assistance from nonprofit foundations or drug makers. Today their assistance often gets absorbed by the plan while they keep paying out of pocket; under the bill, that money counts and can get them to their out-of-pocket maximum.

how_it_helps.text: Requires health plans and insurers to count amounts paid by or on behalf of a patient — including assistance from nonprofit organizations and prescription drug manufacturers — toward the patient's deductible, coinsurance, copayment, and out-of-pocket limit.
The rules apply specifically to specialty drugs and to drugs subject to utilization management, the categories where patients most often rely on third-party copay help.
Creates a tax-code safe harbor so health plans can count drug-assistance payments toward high-deductible health plan minimums without losing that tax status.
The changes would apply to group health plans and insurers for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2026.

analysis.who_pays: Health plans and insurers, who would absorb more drug costs once third-party assistance counts toward out-of-pocket limits; some of that cost would likely flow into premiums for all enrollees. Drug manufacturers keep paying for the copay cards, but the bill makes those cards more effective at keeping patients on brand-name drugs rather than cheaper alternatives.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health plans, and premiums for everyone

drawbacks.text: Counting manufacturer copay-card money toward out-of-pocket limits can push patients toward costlier brand-name drugs over cheaper generics and biosimilars, and the added costs to plans tend to be recouped through higher premiums spread across all enrollees — a long-standing objection to copay-accumulator bans.
The bill explicitly preserves plan utilization-management tools such as prior authorization and step therapy, so patients can still face delays before getting the drug their assistance applies to.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the patients this bill targets — people whose charity or manufacturer assistance currently evaporates against a deductible they can never reach — the benefit is direct and substantial, and the bipartisan, across-the-ideology sponsorship reflects that. The honest cost is that some of the added burden on plans returns as somewhat higher premiums for everyone, and manufacturer copay cards, which the bill validates, are themselves a tool that keeps drug prices high. Whether the patient relief outweighs the premium effect depends on how many plans currently run accumulator programs; the bill does not address underlying drug prices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate health committee, sat there for about a year, got one hearing in March 2026, and still has not been brought up for a committee vote or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall introduced the bill on March 5, 2025, joined by original cosponsors from both parties: Sens. Kaine, Tillis, Markey, Murkowski, and Merkley.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
The bill attracted 27 cosponsors — 20 Democrats and 7 Republicans — but the committee held only a hearing, on March 19, 2026, and has not scheduled a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has changed position: health plans can continue their current copay-accumulator practices, and patients waiting for relief have gotten nothing. The status quo favors the payers.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship is 20 Democrats and 7 Republicans, with original sponsorship split evenly across the ideological spectrum (Marshall, Tillis, Murkowski on the right; Markey, Merkley, Kaine on the left) — no record of opposition votes, since the bill has not reached one.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: Plans that currently keep patients' third-party copay assistance without counting it toward deductibles or out-of-pocket maximums would have to credit it, absorbing more of patients' drug costs. Their savings under current practice come directly out of patients' pockets, so their interest here runs against the public's.

The bill validates manufacturer copay assistance as money that counts toward cost-sharing, making copay cards a more effective tool for keeping patients on brand-name drugs instead of cheaper generics. Individual patients get short-term relief, but the mechanism props up high list prices.
Charities that pay patients' drug copays become far more effective when their donations actually reduce what patients owe, rather than being absorbed by the plan.

analysis.trajectory: With roughly a year left in this Congress, the bill has unusually broad bipartisan sponsorship but only a hearing to show for it. Most bills at this stage die in committee; the realistic paths forward are a HELP committee markup or attachment to a larger health or spending package late in the session. Absent one of those, it will expire with no vote.
